strengths: Addresses a genuinely useful and underexplored problem (high-quality RGBA/transparent video generation) with clear practical applications in content creation and editing.

The VAE design that reuses a frozen pretrained RGB VAE with lightweight LoRA decoders and a causal 3D feature-merge block is a reasonable and efficient engineering approach that avoids training a large model from scratch.

The combination of soft/hard rendering losses (reconstruction, perceptual, edge/Sobel) for training the alpha-aware VAE is a sensible multi-objective design that targets known failure modes such as blurred or inaccurate alpha edges.

The method reports substantial efficiency gains at inference (4-step sampling without CFG, no extra computational cost vs. base Wan model, ~15x faster than the open TransPixeler baseline), which is a meaningful practical contribution if verified.

Qualitative results across many examples (fire, glass, hair, semi-transparent fabric, glowing effects) show visually convincing transparency rendering and are more diverse than typically shown in prior RGBA video papers.
The authors plan to release the pretrained model, which would benefit reproducibility and community adoption if it materializes.
weaknesses: No quantitative evaluation whatsoever: there are no metrics (e.g., FID/FVD, LPIPS, alpha-specific metrics like SAD/MSE/gradient error, or CLIP-based text-video alignment scores) anywhere in the paper, including for the VAE reconstruction quality or the final text-to-video generation. All comparisons to TransPixeler and qualitative claims of 'superior performance' rest entirely on a handful of hand-picked example videos and figures, which is insufficient evidence for a top-tier venue and is susceptible to cherry-picking.
No user study or any systematic comparison protocol (e.g., number of test prompts, statistical significance) is described; the comparison section only shows 7 example prompts against TransPixeler.

No ablation studies to justify individual design choices: e.g., the contribution of each loss term (L_rec, L_per, L_edge) in Eq. 7-13, the effect of hard vs. soft rendering supervision, the choice of DoRA vs. LoRA for the diffusion transformer (the paper claims DoRA is better but shows no supporting comparison), or the impact of feature-merge block architecture choices (causal 3D conv vs. alternatives).

The training data for the diffusion transformer (T2V stage) is extremely small — only 437 curated video/image samples total (301 videos + 20 images + 116 special-effect videos) — raising concerns about generalization, overfitting, and diversity of the final model, which is not discussed or tested beyond a limited set of qualitative examples.

No comparison against other relevant/recent transparent generation baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., AlphaVAE, LayerAnimate, TransAnimate, TransVDM, LayerDiff) despite citing them; only TransPixeler is compared, and only qualitatively.

The paper does not report standard efficiency/quality trade-off numbers in table form (e.g., FLOPs, parameter counts of LoRA/DoRA modules, VRAM usage) to substantiate efficiency claims beyond a single wall-clock comparison on one prompt/hardware setup.

Captions for the training dataset were manually refined in Chinese only, and the model is evaluated using machine-translated English prompts for TransPixeler baseline prompts; this raises concerns about fair comparison, since translation artifacts could bias qualitative outcomes in either direction, and this is not discussed as a potential confound.
The Limitations section is very brief and only shows two failure figures (inaccurate alpha masks, unintended background elements) without deeper analysis of failure rates or root causes.

Overall technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the VAE design largely follows LayerDiffuse's paradigm (embed alpha into RGB latent space) adapted with LoRA/causal convolutions for video, and the T2V training follows standard DoRA fine-tuning of the Wan backbone; the main contributions are engineering/data-centric rather than a fundamentally new method, which would be more acceptable if paired with rigorous quantitative validation, which is missing.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant and underexplored problem (high-quality RGBA/transparent text-to-video generation) and proposes a reasonably clean engineering solution: reusing a frozen pretrained RGB VAE/DiT with lightweight LoRA/DoRA adapters to add alpha-channel modeling, which keeps inference cost essentially unchanged compared to prior work (TransPixeler) that doubles cost via token duplication.

The VAE design (feature-merge block with causal 3D convolution, soft/hard rendering losses, perceptual and edge losses) is technically sensible and well described, and the paper carefully documents the multi-source data curation and captioning pipeline used for both VAE and diffusion training.

Qualitative results (Figs. 1, 10-18) show visibly sharper alpha edges (e.g., hair, fur), more coherent semi-transparent/glow effects, and fewer artifacts than the baseline TransPixeler in the shown examples, and the reported 15x faster inference than the open TransPixeler baseline is a meaningful practical advantage if reproducible.
The authors are transparent about failure cases (inaccurate/incomplete alpha masks, spurious background artifacts), which is a positive for scientific honesty.
weaknesses: No quantitative evaluation whatsoever: the entire comparison to TransPixeler and all internal analyses rely exclusively on a handful of hand-picked qualitative examples (7 prompts total in the main comparison). There are no standard metrics for video/image quality (FVD, FID, CLIP score, alpha matting metrics like SAD/MSE/Grad, temporal consistency metrics), no user study, and no quantitative VAE reconstruction quality report despite the paper claiming the VAE is a core contribution.

No ablation studies: the paper introduces several design choices (feature merge block with causal 3D conv vs. simpler alternatives, three separate loss terms Lrec/Lper/Ledge, soft- vs hard-rendering supervision, LoRA vs DoRA, rank choices) but never isolates their individual contributions, making it impossible to verify that each design choice is actually necessary or beneficial.

Extremely small and undocumented-in-scale text-to-video training set: only 437 videos (301+20+116) are used to fine-tune the diffusion transformer, yet no analysis is given of how this compares in scale to competing methods, nor any discussion of overfitting risk, diversity limits, or generalization beyond the curated domains (mostly portraits, product-style objects, effects).

The speed comparison (128s vs 32min, '15x faster') is confounded by multiple simultaneous differences (81 vs 49 frames, 832x480 vs 720x480, 16 vs 8 FPS, 4-step vs presumably more sampling steps, LightX2V acceleration, no CFG) making the claimed efficiency gain not a controlled or fair comparison, and it conflates VAE/architecture benefits with orthogonal inference-acceleration tricks (LightX2V, CFG removal) that could equally be applied to baselines.

Captions for the curated dataset were originally created in Chinese and machine-translated for the paper, and the model itself is evaluated with Chinese prompts while baselines use English prompts translated by the authors — this asymmetric evaluation setup could bias qualitative comparisons and is not adequately controlled for.

The 'Limitations' section acknowledges frequent failure modes (holes/missing alpha regions, hallucinated background elements) but these are not quantified in frequency or severity, leaving the reader unable to gauge robustness.

Overall the paper reads largely as a system/engineering report combining existing techniques (LayerDiffuse-style VAE adaptation, LoRA/DoRA, rectified flow, causal 3D conv from Wan-VAE) with a curated dataset, and the core novelty (embedding alpha into RGB latent space via LoRA decoders) is incremental relative to LayerDiffuse and AlphaVAE; without quantitative evidence it is hard to assess whether the claimed 'superior performance' actually holds beyond a cherry-picked set of examples.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-explored problem (high-quality RGBA/alpha-channel video generation), with clear applications in editing, VFX, and content creation.

The technical approach is elegant and efficient: rather than training new encoder/decoder branches from scratch (as LayerDiffuse/TransPixeler do), the method reuses the frozen pretrained Wan VAE and DiT, adding only a lightweight feature-merge block and LoRA/DoRA adapters for both the RGB and alpha decoders and the diffusion transformer. This keeps training/inference cost essentially unchanged relative to the RGB-only backbone, in contrast to TransPixeler's doubled token/attention cost.

The rendering-aware training losses for the VAE (soft-render, hard-render, reconstruction, perceptual, edge/Sobel losses) are a sensible design to jointly supervise RGB and alpha and to handle semi-transparent regions and fine edges (hair, glow, smoke).

Careful, well-documented data curation and captioning pipeline (multi-source matting datasets + manually verified/augmented Chinese captions with explicit attribute tags) is described in useful detail, aiding reproducibility of the data pipeline concept even if the raw data is proprietary.

Qualitative results (Figs. 1, 5-18) show diverse, visually convincing outputs including hair strands, glowing/translucent objects, and complex motions, which are historically difficult cases for transparent video generation.

Practical engineering contributions are highlighted (4-step CFG-free inference, LightX2V acceleration, compatibility with community deployment/acceleration tools), which increase potential usefulness if released.
The paper explicitly reports failure cases (Figs. 19-20), which is good scientific transparency about current limitations.
weaknesses: No quantitative evaluation whatsoever is provided. All comparisons to TransPixeler (Figs. 10-16) and all internal design claims are supported only by qualitative side-by-side frames; there is no PSNR/SSIM/alpha-matting error for VAE reconstruction, no FVD/CLIP-score/FID-style metric for generation quality, and no user study. Claims such as "outperforms in motion consistency, visual quality, alpha edge sharpness, and semi-transparent effects" are stated as if established facts but rest entirely on a handful of cherry-picked examples chosen by the authors, which is weak evidence for a top-tier venue.

No ablation studies are reported for any of the proposed components (feature-merge block design, choice of LoRA vs. full fine-tuning, contribution of L_rec/L_per/L_edge, soft- vs. hard-render supervision, random background-color augmentation, DoRA vs. LoRA for the DiT). Several of these are asserted informally in prose (e.g., "DoRA... yield better semantic alignment... compared to LoRA") without any supporting comparison, numbers, or even qualitative examples.

The efficiency comparison ("15 times faster") is measured only against the open-source TransPixeler implementation, built on a different, older backbone (CogVideoX-5B) at a different resolution/frame count/FPS; this confounds architecture, backbone scale, and implementation-level optimization, making the speed claim not a fair or clean ablation of the proposed design's actual computational saving over doubling tokens.

The final text-to-video training set is extremely small (437 curated clips/images), and no analysis is given of generalization, overfitting risk, or diversity coverage beyond the qualitative gallery; given the model is fine-tuned via DoRA on this small curated set, it is unclear how well it generalizes outside the depicted example categories.

Captions are Chinese-only, with English inputs relying on Wan's underlying multilingual capacity and machine translation for the paper's figures; no analysis is given of English-prompt fidelity, which is relevant since the target community/dataset for CVPR is largely English-prompted.

The reported failure modes (background leakage, holes in alpha masks, semi-transparent inaccuracies for astronauts) are acknowledged but not analyzed quantitatively (e.g., frequency of failure, common causes), limiting insight into robustness.

Comparison against AlfaVAE/LayerDiffuse-based VAEs (the closest architectural baselines beyond TransPixeler) is omitted entirely; only TransPixeler is compared, despite AlphaVAE being explicitly discussed in related work as a strong recent VAE-based competitor.

Method reproducibility for the community is uncertain: while a released model is promised, the training/curated dataset (437 samples), captioning pipeline, and manual labeling process are not going to be released or are not clearly stated as being released, which limits the ability of others to reproduce the T2V fine-tuning step even if the VAE/backbone code is shared.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem (RGB-A video generation) with a clear, well-motivated core idea: shifting the alpha distribution while preserving RGB distribution to reduce RGB-alpha entanglement.

Two complementary technical contributions target both ends of the diffusion process: a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss for the VAE latent space, and a transparency-guided mean sampler for the noise space, giving a coherent end-to-end story.

The bidirectional diffusion loss is a clever way to leverage a frozen pretrained DiT as a proxy for 'distinguishability' rather than relying on a naive explicit distance-based separation, which is a reasonable and somewhat novel mechanism.

Strong empirical results: consistent improvements across all reported VBench-derived metrics (text alignment, aesthetic quality, naturalness, motion smoothness, temporal flickering) and a user study showing clear preference for transparency correctness and overall quality versus TransPixeler, LayerFlow, and LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff baselines.

Practical benefits are demonstrated, including large inference speedups (~15x faster than TransPixeler) by avoiding backbone duplication and enabling compatibility with acceleration tools (LightX2V, few-step sampling).
The Gaussian ellipse mask mechanism provides an interesting and demonstrably useful controllability feature (positioning/sizing of transparent regions) not offered by prior RGB-A video methods.

Careful dataset curation effort (multiple matting sources, captioning, attribute labeling) partially addresses the data scarcity problem central to this task, and the paper commits to releasing the dataset and model.
Ablations (Table 3, Fig. 7, Fig. 8) reasonably isolate the contribution of rendering losses, TABD, and mean sampler, supporting the claimed mechanism.
weaknesses: The RGB-A video generation training dataset is very small (429 curated samples: 301 videos + 43 images + 85 special-effect videos), raising concerns about generalization and the statistical reliability of comparisons; scale and diversity limitations are not discussed critically.

Quantitative metrics in Table 1 rely on renders against a white background and GPT-4o-based naturalness/text-alignment scores plus VBench metrics designed for RGB video, none of which directly measure alpha/transparency accuracy — the paper acknowledges this gap and compensates only with a small-scale user study, whose participant count, demographics, and statistical significance are not reported.

No error bars, variance, or statistical significance testing are given for either quantitative metrics or the user study, making it hard to assess robustness of the claimed 'state-of-the-art across all metrics' claim.

The reconstruction ablation (Table 3) shows fairly small absolute PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS gains from TABD, and no ablation quantitatively isolates the mean-sampler's effect on generation-quality metrics (only qualitative figures are shown for Fig. 7/8/9), limiting confidence in the magnitude of contribution of each component to final video quality.

Method comparisons could be viewed as somewhat asymmetric: the proposed model is trained on the authors' newly curated, higher-quality dataset while baselines (LayerFlow, TransPixeler) were trained on different data/objectives, making it unclear how much of the improvement stems from the algorithmic contributions versus the curated data itself.

The derivation of the Gaussian ellipse mask (mean/covariance/eigen-decomposition of the alpha mask) is somewhat ad hoc and heuristic; its sensitivity to irregular/multi-object alpha shapes or multiple disconnected transparent regions is not analyzed.

The paper does not report failure cases or limitations of the proposed method (e.g., complex multi-object scenes, extreme motion, or highly irregular transparent geometries), which would strengthen the credibility of the claims.
Only a single base model architecture (Wan2.1-T2V-14B) is used; no ablation on whether the method generalizes to other video diffusion backbones, limiting evidence of broader applicability.

Details on training cost/compute, hyperparameter sensitivity of the bidirectional loss weighting, and how mask regions (O, S, T) are precisely thresholded in practice are somewhat under-specified in the main text (deferred to supplementary, not included here).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem (RGB-A video generation) with clear creative-industry applications.

The core idea of separately shifting the alpha distribution while preserving the RGB distribution in both latent (VAE) and noise space is a reasonable and relatively novel framing, distinct from simply duplicating channels or backbones as in prior work (LayerDiffuse-based pipelines, TransPixeler).

The method requires no architectural change to the base video DiT at inference (LoRA/DoRA merge), giving a notable inference speed advantage over TransPixeler (claimed 15x), which is a meaningful practical benefit if reproducible.
Reasonably thorough ablations are provided for VAE reconstruction (rendering losses, TABD) and qualitative ablations for the mean sampler, helping to justify individual design choices.
The paper proposes to release a curated RGB-A dataset with detailed captions and attribute labels, which could be a useful community resource given data scarcity in this space.
Demonstrates an interesting controllability feature (Gaussian ellipse mask for shape/position of transparency) and an extension to image-to-video, broadening the application scope.
weaknesses: The DiT fine-tuning dataset is extremely small (429 total samples: 301 video + 43 image + 85 special-effect videos) for fine-tuning a 14B-parameter video generation model; this raises serious concerns about generalization, overfitting, and the robustness of the reported gains, which the paper does not address with any data-scaling ablation.

The theoretical justification for the bidirectional diffusion loss (simply flipping the sign of the squared RF loss in non-opaque regions) is weak: minimizing a negated squared-error term is unbounded below and could in principle destabilize or degenerate training (e.g., pushing predictions to diverge) unless implicitly regularized by the frozen DiT and other losses; the paper offers no training curves, stability analysis, or discussion of why this does not collapse, despite explicitly claiming that direct distance-maximizing strategies would destabilize training.

Quantitative transparency evaluation is limited to a small VAE reconstruction table (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and a subjective user study (Table 2) with no reported number of participants, trials, or statistical significance; there is no quantitative alpha-matting-specific metric (e.g., SAD, MSE, gradient error against ground-truth alpha) for the end-to-end generation pipeline, which is the central claim of the paper ("stable transparency").

Baseline comparison is narrow: only two prior RGB-A video generation methods (TransPixeler, LayerFlow) plus one self-constructed baseline (LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff) are compared; while this reflects field novelty, it still limits the strength of the SOTA claims, and no ablation isolates how much of the improvement stems from the stronger base model (Wan2.1-14B) versus the proposed distribution-shifting techniques.

Reproducibility is not currently verifiable: the model/dataset are promised for future open-source release but are not provided with the submission, and the method depends on a large proprietary-scale base model (Wan2.1-T2V-14B) and additional tooling (LightX2V, DoRA, GPT-4o-based evaluation), making independent verification difficult.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations or failure-case discussion; given the very small fine-tuning set and simple geometric (ellipse) controllability mechanism, it is unclear how the method behaves on complex multi-object or multi-region transparency scenes, which is not analyzed.

Some notational and presentation issues (e.g., overloaded tilde/hat symbols, inconsistent use of μ as both a learned mean function and a scalar control factor) reduce clarity and could confuse readers attempting to reproduce the method.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear technical gap (RGB/alpha entanglement in shared latent spaces) and proposes two complementary, well-motivated solutions: a bidirectional diffusion loss during VAE training and a transparency-guided mean sampler in the noise space, addressing both ends of the diffusion pipeline.

The bidirectional diffusion loss is a genuinely interesting idea -- using a frozen DiT's likelihood signal to implicitly shape the VAE latent distribution rather than relying on explicit distance-based regularization, which is a more principled way of ensuring the shift is meaningful to the downstream generator.

Comprehensive empirical comparison against the relevant state of the art (TransPixeler open/closed, LayerFlow, LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff), including both quantitative metrics (VBench, GPT-4o-based text alignment/naturalness) and a user study specifically targeting transparency correctness, which existing automated metrics cannot capture.

Ablations (Table 3, Fig. 7-8) isolate the contribution of rendering losses, TABD, and the mean sampler, providing reasonably convincing evidence that each component contributes incrementally to reconstruction and generation quality.

Practical engineering value: the design allows LoRA/DoRA to be merged into the base model with no extra inference cost, and the method is reported to be ~15x faster than TransPixeler while supporting few-step (4-step) sampling, which is a meaningful usability advantage for a creative-tools audience.

The controllability application (Gaussian ellipse mask for shape/position of transparency) and the image-to-video extension demonstrate the method's broader applicability beyond a narrow benchmark setting.
The paper also contributes a curated RGB-A dataset with detailed captions and attribute labels, addressing a real data scarcity problem in this subfield.
weaknesses: The RGB-A video generation fine-tuning dataset is very small (429 curated videos/images), which raises concerns about generalization and about how much of the reported gains stem from the proposed losses versus dataset curation quality versus the strong Wan2.1-14B base model; no ablation isolates the dataset's contribution from the architectural/loss contributions.

There is no direct quantitative evaluation of alpha-channel accuracy against ground-truth mattes for the final generative model (only VAE reconstruction PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS in Table 3); the main comparison table relies on RGB-rendered VBench metrics and a subjective user study, leaving the core transparency-quality claim only weakly quantitatively substantiated.

The ablation on the mean sampler (Sec 4.3, 'Analysis on DiT') is purely qualitative (Fig. 7), without corresponding quantitative metrics analogous to Table 1, making it harder to assess the magnitude of its benefit versus TABD alone.

Baselines may not be perfectly matched in training data/domain (e.g., TransPixeler trained mainly on human matting data), so some of the qualitative failure cases shown for competitors could partly reflect data mismatch rather than purely architectural limitations, which somewhat weakens the fairness of the comparison narrative.

No discussion of failure cases or limitations of the proposed method itself (e.g., behavior under very high semi-transparency density, multiple simultaneous transparent regions, or scenes not well captured by an elliptical Gaussian prior).

Reproducibility is currently only promised (open-source release pending), and given the scale of the underlying model (Wan2.1-14B) and closed-source comparison points, independent verification of results is not presently possible.

The GPT-4o-based text alignment/naturalness metric and VBench scores, while standard, are known to have their own biases; relying heavily on them (with large score gaps, e.g., 4.00 vs 3.45 for text alignment) without inter-rater/metric reliability analysis leaves some uncertainty about the robustness of the reported superiority margins.
